_scope_definitions.all: The paper states it estimates a causal effect of an endogenous regressor using an instrumental variable (2SLS/IV/GMM with an excluded instrument). Fires on any paper that names an instrument for an endogenous regressor. A paper that runs only OLS/regression adjustment and never names an instrument is out of scope.
_scope_definitions.as_if_random_or_conditional: Fires when the paper describes its instrument as randomly or as-if-randomly assigned (lottery/natural experiment), or as valid only conditional on named covariates. Near-miss that does NOT fire: an instrument defended purely by theoretical argument with no claim of (conditional) random assignment.
_scope_definitions.late_causal: The paper states it interprets its IV estimate as an average causal/treatment effect: it invokes potential outcomes or compliers/LATE, or it explicitly allows the treatment effect to vary across units (heterogeneous effects) and reads the 2SLS coefficient as such an average. Fires only on an explicit causal-effect reading. NEAR-MISS that does NOT fire: a paper that explicitly assumes a single constant/homogeneous structural coefficient and reports only that slope, making no complier/average-treatment-effect claim; a purely predictive/first-stage-only exercise. Ambiguity resolves OUT (NA): a coder never infers a causal-effect reading, or effect heterogeneity, the paper did not state.
_scope_definitions.multiple_endogenous: The paper states it instruments two or more endogenous regressors jointly in the same equation. Fires on a declared count >1 of endogenous regressors. NEAR-MISS: a single endogenous regressor with several instruments (overidentified but one endogenous variable) does NOT fire.

claim: A paper must state which causal parameter (estimand) its IV design targets, rather than leaving the estimated quantity implicit.
observable: Whether the paper contains an explicit statement naming the causal parameter being estimated (e.g., the effect of the endogenous regressor on the outcome for a named population).
pass_condition: The paper names, in words, the causal parameter it estimates; where that parameter is population-specific (e.g., a local effect), it also identifies the population it applies to.
flag_condition: The paper reports an IV estimate without ever stating which causal parameter it is meant to identify.
severity_basis: Sources require readers be told the causal parameter estimated before the estimate can be judged (Sovey 2010; Dunning 2012).
requirement_statement: State the target causal parameter the IV estimate is meant to identify.

claim: Because the exclusion restriction cannot be tested from the data, a paper must give a substantive argument for why its instrument affects the outcome only through the endogenous regressor.
observable: Whether the paper presents reasoning (not a statistical test) defending that the instrument has no pathway to the outcome except through the treatment.
pass_condition: The paper gives an explicit substantive argument for the exclusion restriction, findable anywhere in the paper or its appendices.
flag_condition: The paper invokes an instrument but offers no argued defense of the exclusion restriction, or defends it only by an OLS regression of the outcome on the instrument.
severity_basis: Sources make the exclusion restriction the pivotal, untestable IV assumption whose violation biases the estimate (Sovey 2010; Kippersluis 2018; Conley 2010).
requirement_statement: Argue, substantively, why the instrument influences the outcome only through the endogenous regressor.

claim: IV requires the instrument to be (as-if) independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome; outside a clean randomization this ignorability must be argued explicitly.
observable: Whether the paper argues that the instrument is unrelated to outcome confounders / as-good-as-randomly assigned, and (when not physically randomized) makes that case rather than assuming it.
pass_condition: The paper argues the instrument is independent of confounders of the treatment-outcome relationship, e.g. by establishing (conditional) random or as-if-random assignment and naming the conditioning covariates it relies on.
flag_condition: The paper treats a non-randomized instrument as exogenous without argument, or rests independence on an a-priori belief with no supporting reasoning.
severity_basis: Sources hold that a non-random instrument's ignorability must be argued and that an unexamined belief in exogeneity does not make IV credible (Angrist 1996; Bound 1995; Dunning 2012).
requirement_statement: The paper must argue the instrument is (as-if) independent of the outcome's unobserved determinants, explicitly when it is not physically randomized.

claim: When the instrument is claimed to be (conditionally) randomly assigned, that claim has a testable implication: the instrument should be unrelated to predetermined covariates, which the paper should check.
observable: Whether the paper reports comparing the instrument against variables fixed before assignment (a balance / randomization check), using the same covariate scheme it uses in estimation.
pass_condition: The paper reports a balance/randomization check — e.g. tests or comparisons of predetermined covariates across instrument values, or an F-test for unexpected instrument-covariate correlations.
flag_condition: The paper claims (conditional) random or as-if-random assignment but reports no check of the instrument against predetermined covariates.
severity_basis: Sources note random assignment is directly testable by balance tests and that as-if random should be assessed even in lotteries (Frandsen 2022; Dunning 2012).
requirement_statement: A paper claiming (conditional) random assignment must report a balance/randomization check of the instrument against predetermined covariates.

evidence.quote: Random assignment can be directly tested via the usual balance tests, but the exclusion restriction portion of Condition 1(i) cannot be directly verified.

claim: A paper reading its IV estimate as an average treatment effect under possibly heterogeneous effects must justify monotonicity (that the instrument moves no unit's treatment in the opposite direction — no defiers).
observable: Whether the paper states and defends the monotonicity/no-defiers condition (by argument or design).
pass_condition: A paper with a fired late_causal trigger gives a theoretical or design-based justification that no defiers exist.
flag_condition: A late_causal paper interprets the IV estimand as an average effect without addressing monotonicity.
severity_basis: Without monotonicity the IV estimand is not a nonnegatively-weighted average of treatment effects (Imbens 1994; Angrist 1996; Gelman 2006). A coder decides fired-vs-not from the paper's stated causal-effect reading alone; an unfired or ambiguous trigger is NA.
requirement_statement: Justify monotonicity (no defiers) when interpreting the IV estimand as an average treatment effect.

claim: IV rests on the stable-unit-treatment-value assumption of no interference between units; spillovers between treated and untreated units bias the estimate, so the paper should address them.
observable: Whether the paper addresses no-interference / SUTVA -- by arguing that one unit's outcome is unaffected by other units' assignment or treatment, or by explicitly modeling spillovers where they are expected.
pass_condition: The paper addresses no interference between units -- arguing from design or context that one unit's outcome is unaffected by other units' assignment/treatment, or explicitly modeling the interference where it is expected.
flag_condition: The paper neither argues no interference between units nor models spillovers -- it is silent on SUTVA.
severity_basis: Sources state SUTVA is required and that settings where it is implausible cannot use standard IV, with spillovers biasing estimates in an unpredictable direction (Angrist 1996; Sovey 2010).
requirement_statement: The paper must address no interference between units (SUTVA), by argument, design, or explicit modeling.

evidence.quote: we follow the convention in statistics and medical research by assuming no interference between units.

claim: A paper reading its IV estimate causally under heterogeneity must acknowledge that the estimand is local (compliers / instrument-moved units) and not automatically the population effect.
observable: Whether the paper states that its IV estimate applies only to the subpopulation the instrument moves and flags the resulting limit on generalizability.
pass_condition: A fired late_causal paper states the locality of its estimand (compliers / instrument-shifted range) and does not silently generalize it to the whole population.
flag_condition: A late_causal paper presents its IV estimate as a population/average effect with no acknowledgment of complier-locality.
severity_basis: IV identifies an effect only for instrument-responsive units, which need not equal the population effect (Imbens 1994; Gelman 2006; Angrist 1996; Sovey 2010). Trigger fired-vs-not is decided from the paper's own causal reading; ambiguity is NA.
requirement_statement: Acknowledge the local (complier) nature of the IV estimand and its limited generalizability.

claim: A paper must report a first-stage instrument-strength diagnostic (first-stage F and/or partial R-squared of the excluded instruments net of covariates).
observable: Whether the paper reports a first-stage strength statistic for the excluded instrument(s).
pass_condition: The paper reports a first-stage F statistic or partial R-squared of the excluded instruments (partialling out covariates), findable anywhere in the paper or appendices.
flag_condition: The paper reports IV/2SLS estimates but no first-stage strength statistic.
severity_basis: Weak instruments produce large finite-sample bias and unreliable inference; sources require applied work to report first-stage strength as a matter of routine (Staiger-Stock 1997; Bound 1995).
prevalence_aggravator: Surveys find IV papers routinely omit any first-stage relevance statistic (Staiger-Stock 1997; Sovey 2010).
requirement_statement: Report a first-stage instrument-strength statistic (F or partial R-squared of the excluded instruments).

evidence.quote: first stage F statistics (or, when n > 1, GT and/or the bias measures in Section 3b) should be reported

When Equations (1) and (2) include common exogenous variables, the relevant parameter is the partial R2, the pop- ulation R2 from the regression of x on z once the common exogenous variables have been partialled out of both x and z.

claim: When the first stage is weak, a paper must use identification-robust inference (e.g., Anderson-Rubin / effective-F-based procedures) rather than conventional t/Wald intervals, which under-cover; rescaling standard errors does not fix this.
observable: Whether, given a weak first stage, the paper reports weak-instrument-robust inference rather than relying only on conventional 2SLS standard errors.
pass_condition: Either the first-stage effective F is at or above the strong-instrument threshold (23.1, the conservative worst-case value for TSLS) and conventional inference is reported; or the effective F is weak/borderline and the paper additionally reports weak-instrument-robust inference (e.g., an Anderson-Rubin confidence set).
flag_condition: The first-stage effective F is below the strong-instrument threshold and the paper reports only conventional t/Wald standard errors or CIs, with no identification-robust inference.
severity_basis: Under weak instruments conventional IV t-statistics are non-normal and CIs miss nominal coverage at any sample size; correct coverage needs test inversion, not rescaled SEs (Staiger-Stock 1997; Andrews-Stock-Sun 2019; Stock-Wright-Yogo 2002).

threshold.band_rule: Judge strength on the first-stage EFFECTIVE F (not an ordinary F against homoskedastic critical values; see IV-INFER-03). At or above 23.1 (the conservative worst-case effective-F critical value for TSLS) conventional inference alone PASSes; below 10 the first stage is weak and a weak-instrument-robust confidence set is required to PASS; within [10, 23.1] strength is not established at the conservative bound, so PASS only if a weak-instrument-robust confidence set is also reported, otherwise FLAG.

requirement_statement: Use identification-robust inference when the first stage is weak.

evidence.quote: we cannot obtain correct coverage under weak instruments by adjusting our (finite) standard errors, and so points to the need for a different approach such as test inversion
will not in general have a 95% coverage rate, even asymptotically
If instruments are weak, then the sampling distributions of GMM and IV statistics are in general nonnormal
Thus, a simple, asymptotically valid rule of thumb is available for TSLS that rejects when the effective F is greater than 23.1.

claim: Under non-homoskedastic, clustered, or serially correlated errors, instrument strength must be judged with an error-structure-matched robust weak-instrument statistic (the effective F), not by comparing an ordinary or robust first-stage F to homoskedastic Stock-Yogo critical values.
observable: Whether the strength diagnostic the paper uses matches its error structure (effective / robust weak-instrument statistic) rather than an ordinary F judged against homoskedastic critical values.
pass_condition: With non-homoskedastic/clustered/serial errors, the paper assesses strength with a heteroskedasticity/HAC/cluster-robust weak-instrument statistic (e.g., effective F).
flag_condition: The paper has non-homoskedastic/clustered/serial errors but judges strength by an ordinary (or plain robust) first-stage F against homoskedastic Stock-Yogo values.
severity_basis: Outside the homoskedastic serially-uncorrelated case the ordinary/robust F has no theoretical basis as a strength measure and Stock-Yogo mappings break down (Montiel Olea-Pflueger 2013; Andrews-Stock-Sun 2019).
requirement_statement: Assess instrument strength with an error-structure-matched robust statistic (effective F), not a plain F against homoskedastic critical values.

evidence.quote: to the best of our knowledge, there is no analysis supporting this practice.

claim: A paper must not select or discard specifications by a first-stage F threshold, because F-screening biases the surviving estimates and distorts test size.
observable: Whether the paper reports keeping/dropping specifications, samples, or instruments on the basis of a first-stage F cutoff.
pass_condition: The paper does not screen specifications on a first-stage F threshold (silence about such screening passes).
flag_condition: The paper states it retained only specifications, samples, or instruments whose first-stage F exceeded a cutoff.
severity_basis: Discarding specifications by a first-stage F threshold worsens rather than mitigates weak-instrument inference, biasing estimates and distorting size for any F variant (Andrews-Stock-Sun 2019).
requirement_statement: Do not screen/select specifications by a first-stage F threshold.

evidence.quote: While selection on first-stage F-statistics is intuitively reasonable, it can unfortunately result in bias in published estimates and size distortions in published tests
screening on the first-stage F-statistic appears to compound, rather than reduce, inferential problems arising from weak instruments

claim: A paper must match its variance/standard-error estimator to the error and clustering structure of the data (clustering at the level of dependence; adjusting for the two stages / generated regressors), so reported IV standard errors are valid.
observable: Whether the reported IV standard errors use a variance estimator appropriate to the design's heteroskedasticity/clustering/serial-correlation and account for the estimation stages.
pass_condition: The paper reports standard errors from a variance estimator matched to its error structure (e.g., clustered at the dependence level; HAC for time series) and consistent with the two-stage/generated-regressor structure.
flag_condition: The paper uses default/homoskedastic or mismatched-level standard errors where the design implies clustering or serial correlation, or ignores the two-stage estimation.
severity_basis: Group-level assignment and unmatched clustering understate uncertainty, and naive second-stage SEs ignore first-stage estimation (Dunning 2012; Sovey 2010; Andrews-Stock-Sun 2019; Gelman 2006).
requirement_statement: Use a variance estimator matched to the error/clustering structure and the two-stage design.

claim: With more than one endogenous regressor, a paper must assess joint identification with a statistic designed for that case (Cragg-Donald minimum-eigenvalue / conditional Sanderson-Windmeijer F), not each equation's own first-stage F.
observable: Whether a paper with multiple endogenous regressors reports a joint/conditional identification statistic rather than only per-equation F statistics.
pass_condition: A fired multiple_endogenous paper reports a Cragg-Donald and/or conditional (Sanderson-Windmeijer) first-stage statistic.
flag_condition: A multiple_endogenous paper judges strength only from separate per-equation first-stage F statistics.
severity_basis: Each equation's F can be large while the reduced-form matrix is near a rank reduction, leaving some parameters underidentified (Sanderson-Windmeijer 2015; Stock-Wright-Yogo 2002).
requirement_statement: Assess joint identification with a Cragg-Donald/conditional-F statistic under multiple endogenous regressors.
